e.t: This noun means “purity”—a clean or undefiled condition. It describes the quality of being pure, especially in relation to a person’s life, worship, or dedication. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages in Numbers, 2 Chronicles, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains purity rather than a specific action or object.

This noun refers to a person who is the “next of kin”—a close family relative recognized as nearest in family relation. It identifies a person’s kinship position rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, mostly in Ruth, with one occurrence in 2 Samuel. The surrounding passage determines what role that next of kin has in a particular verse; the word itself establishes the family relationship.

This noun means “soot,” the dark powdery substance produced by smoke or burning. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus 9, at Exodus 9:8 and Exodus 9:10. The word names a physical substance rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the residue associated with smoke or fire.

Airem, also rendered Erem, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament and appears once, in Joshua 15:52. Because proper names generally identify rather than describe, its significance comes from the person or place it names and from the surrounding passage, not from a broader definition like a common noun or verb. The name itself is preserved as “Airem; Erem.”

This Greek LXX verb means “exhausted; weary,” describing a person who has become worn out or drained. It refers to a condition of fatigue rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, including two occurrences in Psalms and one each in Daniel and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “unhindered”: it describes something that is not blocked, restrained, or prevented from proceeding. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:23, and its ordinary sense remains clear even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. The word alone does not identify what might otherwise hinder the subject; that depends on the surrounding sentence.

This adjective means “unfading”: it describes something that does not fade or lose its lasting quality. It points to what remains fresh, bright, or enduring rather than weakening with time. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Wisdom 6:12. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being described, but its central sense is clear: something lasting and undiminished.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something dim, faint, or only dimly seen. It points to limited clarity or reduced brightness rather than something plainly visible. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, with most occurrences in Leviticus 13. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a lack of clear visibility or brightness.

This Greek LXX verb means “clothe”: to put clothing on someone or provide covering. It describes the act of dressing or covering a person, rather than the garment itself. In the Greek text of Job, it occurs twice, in Job 29:14 and Job 31:19. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the action of clothing or covering.

This Greek LXX verb means “light up,” describing the act of making something shine or become bright. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including passages from Ezekiel, Hosea, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. The precise force—whether something is physically brightened or described with this image—depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains causing or becoming illuminated.

This noun means “fortified wall” or “fortification,” referring to a strengthened defensive barrier. It describes more than an ordinary wall: its basic idea is a structure made secure for protection. Within the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs only twice, in 2 Chronicles and Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains a fortified or defensive wall.

This Greek LXX verb means “overturn” or “turn up/back.” It describes an action of turning something over, reversing its position, or directing it back. As a verb, it expresses movement or change rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 99 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its precise force can vary with the sentence and object involved. Its earliest recorded occurrence is in Genesis 8:11, and it continues through 3 Maccabees 2:30.

This noun refers to recompense or rendering—something given back in return for what has been done or received. It can describe repayment, a returned benefit, or a deserved response, whether favorable or unfavorable. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 16 times across 16 verses, especially in Psalms and Isaiah. Its central idea is a fitting return: what is rendered back corresponds to an earlier action, gift, or debt. The surrounding verse determines whether that return is understood as reward, repayment, or retribution.

This noun describes licentiousness—outrageous behavior that rejects proper restraint and moral order. It names conduct that is openly excessive, shameless, or offensively defiant rather than merely a private mistake or weakness. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Wisdom and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains behavior marked by brazen disregard for what is right and appropriate.

e.h: An Interjection for Himself or Then
e.t: This Greek LXX interjection can mean “he himself; then.” It may point emphatically to the person himself, or mark a transition to what happens next. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 2 Kings. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic function is brief and connective rather than a description of an object, action, or character. It is therefore best understood as a small spoken expression that directs attention to a person or moves the statement forward.

Aōth, also rendered Aoth, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a proper name in the Greek Septuagint and identifies one named individual in the biblical record. This name appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:10. Because the available information gives the name and reference but not the verse text, its specific role in that genealogy must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Beērōtha” or “Virotha.” It identifies a named place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Joshua 18:25. The available information establishes its function as a place-name, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its specific role in that passage.

Gabaath, also rendered Gavaath, is a proper name for a place in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general descriptive word but a specific place-name. The name occurs three times in the Greek LXX, appearing twice in Joshua and once in Judges. Its recorded occurrences are in Joshua 24:33 and Judges 7:1, though the available information does not include the surrounding verse text needed to describe each passage’s particular use.

This word is a proper name rendered “Geddour” or “Yeththur.” It identifies a particular named person, place, or other entity rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs five times, across four verses, with occurrences in 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, its precise referent must be identified from the context of each passage.

Gorgias is a proper name referring to a person named Gorgias. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs eleven times across ten verses, all in 1 and 2 Maccabees. It is consistently rendered “Gorgias,” so it functions as a personal designation rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. The listed occurrences begin at 1 Maccabees 3:38 and extend to 2 Maccabees 12:37; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain what this person does in any particular passage.

This verb means “rise up” or “arise”—to get up or stand up. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Deuteronomy, showing a straightforward action of rising. It occurs in Deuteronomy 6:7 and 11:19, where the surrounding passages provide the fuller setting. Its basic sense remains an upward movement or getting up, rather than a special title, object, or abstract quality.

This noun refers to a sale made to various purchasers—the act or arrangement of transferring something to different buyers. Its meaning is specific: it describes the transaction itself, not simply a person who buys or sells. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 25:33, so its normal sense is established by this single recorded use and its direct definition. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is the personal name Dina, also rendered Thina. It identifies a woman rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times in 11 verses, chiefly in Genesis and once in Job. The name first appears in Genesis 30:21 and is used repeatedly in Genesis 34. Since it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily its reference to the individual named Dina; the surrounding passage is needed to understand what is being said about her in any particular verse.

Drimylos is a proper name, also rendered “Thrimilos.” It identifies a particular named individual or place rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 1:3. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, the name’s exact referent cannot be identified here. Its basic meaning is therefore its role as a distinctive personal or place-name, not a translatable common noun.

This noun means “jettisoning”—the act of throwing something away or casting it off. It names the action itself rather than the person performing it or the object being discarded. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus 11:1 and Jonah 1:5. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being cast away, but the word’s central sense remains the deliberate removal or throwing away of something.

This verb means to train carefully—to practice or prepare something with focused attention and discipline. It describes deliberate cultivation rather than a casual or occasional effort. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 15:12; without the verse text, its specific application there cannot be stated. Its central idea remains careful training: repeated, purposeful preparation aimed at becoming skilled or ready for a task. The word therefore emphasizes the manner of preparation, not merely the fact that preparation takes place.

This word means “eunuch,” a noun used to identify a person by that designation. It names an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or place. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at Leviticus 22:24. The verse text and surrounding passage would be needed to explain its particular role there; its basic lexical meaning remains “eunuch.”

This Greek LXX verb means to “cherish” or “nourish”—to care for someone or something by sustaining and tending it. It can describe providing what is needed for life, as well as giving attentive care that expresses affection. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with uses ranging from nourishment to the tender care of people. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on who or what receives this care and the surrounding sentence.

Elbōn, also rendered Elvon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a place or location in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Joshua 19:28. Because the available wording gives the name but no further definition, its significance is limited to identifying the named location; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its role in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “draw” or “drag”: to pull something or someone from one place toward another. It describes an action exerted on an object or person, whether the movement is willing or forced. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is broader than any single passage. The surrounding verse determines whether the action involves ordinary movement, physical force, or figurative attraction.

This LXX word means “in the face; facing.” It describes something positioned before another person or thing, or expresses being in someone’s presence. Depending on the sentence, it can function as an adjective, adverb, or preposition, helping identify the direction or position of one thing in relation to another. It is broadly used across the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, occurring 457 times, so its precise English rendering depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “come in besides”: it describes entering in addition to someone or something already present. It is an action word, focusing on movement into a place or situation rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 16:16. Without the verse text, its precise force there cannot be described further. Its central idea is entering in addition to what is already present.

This verb means “take in hand; attempt”: it describes undertaking something or trying to carry it out. It presents an action as a person’s deliberate effort, whether or not the effort succeeds. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 11 times, including passages from the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what action is being undertaken there, but its central idea remains beginning or attempting a task. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood separately from similarly rendered words in other biblical language traditions.

This noun refers to a heron, a type of bird. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Psalms. Its basic meaning remains the name of the bird itself; the particular significance of each occurrence must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage. The word is rendered “heron” where an English rendering is available.

This noun means “conscientiousness”: careful, serious attention to what is right or required. It describes an inward quality of responsible care rather than a physical action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Joshua, Proverbs, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains conscientious concern and faithful seriousness.

This verb means “spring on,” describing a sudden leap or rush onto someone or something. It presents an active movement rather than a static condition, so the word focuses on what a person or creature does. In the Greek LXX, it occurs three times, all in 1 Samuel, indicating a specific action word used in a small number of passages. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and event.

This Greek LXX verb means “yoke”: to join animals or people together for a shared task or movement. Its ordinary sense comes from placing two under one yoke so they act together. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across seven verses, including passages involving animals prepared for use or transport. The word describes an action rather than a person or object, and its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

“We” refers to the speaker together with one or more other people. This pronoun identifies a group that includes the person speaking, whether the speaker acts, speaks, belongs, or is described along with others. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 161 times, showing its ordinary use for a collective first-person subject or group. Its exact reference—who is included in “we”—comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

“Thailam” or “Thelam” is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a specific name rather than a general description, action, or quality. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Samuel 3:12. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise referent cannot be identified here; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself, not whether it refers to a person, place, or group.

Tharchna is a proper name, referring to a person named Tharchna or Tharkhna. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament data, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:48. The available wording identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific role or connection in that passage.

Iarbal, also rendered Iarval, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Judges 7:1. The available lexical meaning identifies the name itself, but does not provide an additional definition or explanation of the person named. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage and the verse’s context.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Ioudas” or “Iuthas.” It identifies people rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 245 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 2 Maccabees. Its repeated use across genealogies, narratives, and historical accounts shows that it functions as a person’s name; the particular individual must be identified from the surrounding passage. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX name and should not be treated as a common noun or translated concept.

Iōkan, also rendered Iokan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 1:42. Because it is a proper name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it names a person in the biblical record. The name itself does not provide a general teaching or description apart from the person it identifies.

This noun refers to a necklace or collar worn around the neck. In the Greek Old Testament, it names a piece of personal adornment rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice, once in Isaiah and once in Ezekiel, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. It describes an ornament placed around the neck, and its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “bear fruit”: to produce fruit or bring forth a yield. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so the surrounding sentence determines what is bearing fruit and what kind of fruit is meant. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice—once in Habakkuk and once in Wisdom—so it is an uncommon word in this collection. Its core idea remains the same: fruit is being produced.

This Greek LXX verb means “polish”: to smooth or finish a surface by rubbing it. It describes an action performed on something rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Epistle of Jeremiah 1:7. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage cannot be explained further; its established lexical sense remains the act of polishing or smoothing.

Kezib, also called Keziv, is a proper name for a place rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 15:44. The available wording identifies the place by name but does not provide a further definition or description of its location or significance. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse text.

Kenereth is a proper name: it identifies a particular named entity rather than describing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word appears once, and its recorded rendering is “Kenereth.” The name is found at Joshua 19:35, but its specific significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone. It is distinct from ordinary descriptive vocabulary.

This Greek verb means “sweep” or “sweep out,” describing the act of clearing something away with a sweeping motion. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 31:20. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but the word itself centers on removing or clearing away by sweeping.

This noun means a “mixing vessel,” a container used to combine liquids or prepare a mixture. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears seven times, including descriptions of sacred furnishings and a vessel associated with preparing a meal. The word identifies the container itself rather than the act of mixing or the substance inside it. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Marmasima is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament translation, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its lexical definition is simply “Marmasima,” so the available information identifies the name but does not provide an additional meaning or translation synonym. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Esther 9:9, with no broader usage pattern available. The name should therefore be understood at this basic level without assigning it a context-specific role.

Massēphath, also rendered Massifath, is a proper name for a location rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across eight verses, appearing in 1 Samuel and 2 Kings. The name is especially concentrated in 1 Samuel 7, where it is used repeatedly for the same place-name. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “wardrobe,” referring to a place or furnishing used for keeping clothing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 10:22. Because the word appears only once and the verse text is not included here, its exact practical reference in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning remains a wardrobe: a storage place associated with garments or clothing.

gl: hate the wicked; hate the wickedness
d: hate the wicked; hate the wickedness

e.t: This verb means to hate the wicked or to hate wickedness. It expresses active rejection of evil rather than simple dislike. As a verb, it describes what someone does toward wicked people or wicked conduct. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains opposition to what is wicked.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Moorai” or “Moore.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:30. Since it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily its role as an identifying name; the surrounding verse supplies the information about the person being named.

Nathanael, also rendered Nathanel, is a proper name used to identify people rather than describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 13 times across 13 verses, with occurrences in Numbers, Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The name is applied to individuals in Israel’s genealogical and tribal records. Its exact reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

Ner is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 17 times across 17 verses, from 1 Samuel through 1 Chronicles. The name is associated with people mentioned in Israel’s historical records, so its precise identification depends on the surrounding passage. As a proper name, Ner does not carry a general sentence meaning like a common noun or verb; it identifies an individual named Ner.

This verb means “suppose” or “expect”: it expresses what someone considers likely or assumes to be true. It describes a person’s thought or expectation rather than an action being performed. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 15 times, all in deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the person is supposing or expecting in that surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “rasor,” referring to a sharp tool used to cut or remove hair. It names the implement itself rather than an action or quality. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages associated with shaving, cutting hair, or using a razor as an image of removal. Its occurrences extend from Numbers through Ezekiel, showing a consistent practical meaning. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic reference remains a razor or shaving instrument.

This adjective means “fewest,” describing the smallest number or amount within a comparison. It identifies something as having fewer members, people, or things than the others being considered. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, the Psalms, Isaiah, Amos, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what group or amount is being compared, but its central sense remains the lowest quantity among those under discussion.

“Admittedly” marks something the speaker recognizes or concedes as true. It introduces an acknowledgment, often preparing the reader to consider what follows in light of that accepted point. As an adverb, it modifies a statement by signaling agreement or admission rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees.

This word describes someone who is “quick to anger; choleric.” As an adjective, it characterizes a person or temperament marked by a fast, heated response. It points to an easily provoked disposition rather than a momentary feeling alone. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in Proverbs 14:17. Its precise force in that verse is understood through the surrounding proverb, but its central meaning is a person who becomes angry quickly.

This word means “where.” It points to a place or location and can connect a statement with the place being discussed. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 3,563 times, so it is a common term used across many kinds of passages. Its precise force in any sentence depends on what place or location the surrounding words identify.

This Greek LXX verb means to make things alternate or to transpose them. It describes changing the order or arrangement of things so that one takes another’s place. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in this corpus, including passages in 1 Kings, Ezra, Esther, Proverbs, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being rearranged.

This noun means “exasperation”: a state of intense irritation, especially when patience has been worn down. It names the feeling itself rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word occurs once, at Psalm 94:8. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the inner condition of exasperation or mounting irritation.

This Greek LXX noun means “chamber,” referring to an enclosed room or designated interior space. It is used for chambers connected with temple or household arrangements, storage, and other ordered areas. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Chronicles, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense remains a chamber or room.

This noun refers to a plain—an open, generally level area of land. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it is used for geographic settings rather than for an abstract idea. The word occurs 151 times, showing that it is a common term for describing the physical landscape. Its exact significance in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

This noun means “circumcision,” the physical cutting away of the foreskin. In the Greek Old Testament, it names the bodily practice associated with the covenant sign given to Abraham and his descendants. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Genesis, Exodus, and Jeremiah. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it occurs, while the surrounding passage determines what is being said about the practice or its significance.

This noun refers to “repletion; satisfaction”—a condition of being filled or having enough. It describes fullness rather than an action, and it can concern the satisfaction that comes from provision or abundance. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 26 times, showing a recurring description of being satisfied or filled. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “old one,” referring to a person advanced in age. It functions as a noun or adjective, so it can identify an elderly person or describe someone as old. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 34 times, showing a recurring term for age and older people. Its basic meaning remains focused on age rather than automatically expressing honor, weakness, wisdom, or authority; those ideas must come from the surrounding passage.

This LXX Greek verb means burdened: it describes someone or something being weighed down or becoming a burden. Its basic sense concerns carrying an oppressive load, whether literally or in the broader condition of being heavily burdened. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented in this corpus, so it expresses a recurring condition rather than a rare or highly specialized idea. The surrounding verse determines what produces the burden in each passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “excrement,” referring to bodily waste. It names something expelled from the body rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 32:6. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact figurative or contextual force in that passage cannot be described beyond this basic meaning.

This adjective means “wheat-bearing,” describing something associated with bearing or carrying wheat. It identifies a quality rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Obadiah 1:18. The word’s central idea is therefore simple: it characterizes something as producing, holding, or marked by wheat, while the surrounding verse determines its precise reference. Its meaning remains focused on wheat as what is borne.

This verb means “sprinkle”: to scatter or apply a small amount of liquid in drops. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes an action performed on something or someone, so the word focuses on the act of distributing liquid rather than merely possessing or pouring it. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages from Leviticus, 2 Kings, and Psalms. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on what is being sprinkled and the surrounding passage.

gl: lower part of the back; chine
d: lower part of the back; chine

e.t: This noun refers to the lower part of the back, or the chine—the area along the back of a person or animal. It names a physical body region rather than an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Samuel and Job. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the lower back or backbone area.

This Greek LXX noun means “saviour” or “deliverer”—one who rescues or brings someone out of danger or trouble. It identifies a person by the help he provides, rather than describing an action alone. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek Deuterocanonical writings represented here, including four occurrences in Psalms and one in 3 Maccabees. Its repeated rendering as “deliverer” supports the central idea of rescue. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Samala is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Genesis 36, in verses 36 and 37. The name itself does not carry a broader lexical meaning in the information available here; its function is to identify an individual. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This proper name refers to a place called “Sēgōr” or “Sigor.” It is a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its basic meaning is the identity of that location. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times in eight verses, from Genesis through Isaiah. The name appears especially in Genesis, and it is also found in Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, and Isaiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means "want of corn," referring to a lack or shortage of grain. It describes a condition in which people do not have enough grain for food. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, once in Leviticus and once in Nehemiah. Its basic meaning is therefore practical and concrete: an insufficiency of grain, whether understood as scarcity or the resulting lack of food. The surrounding verse determines the particular circumstances, but the word itself points specifically to grain shortage.

This Greek LXX noun means “earnestness; care displayed”—serious, attentive concern expressed through one’s actions. It describes more than a passing feeling: it points to purposeful diligence and visible care. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 1:9, but the verse text is not available here, so its precise force in that sentence must be determined from the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “turning,” referring to a change of direction or movement. It names the act or process of turning rather than describing a person or object. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including Proverbs, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its central idea remains a turning or change in direction.

This verb means “strike together,” describing the act of bringing blows together or hitting in concert. It expresses a forceful, joined action rather than a quiet meeting or simple agreement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 24:10. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains an action of striking together.

This verb means to “conclude” or “reconcile”: to bring something to a settled understanding or agreement. It can describe reaching a conclusion, arranging agreement between people, or helping someone grasp what should be understood. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times in nine verses, from Exodus through Isaiah, and its uses concern communication, judgment, instruction, and understanding. The exact shade of meaning depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea is bringing thought, speech, or disagreement toward a settled result.

Sychem, also called Sikhem, is a proper name for a place in the Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographic name used to identify a location in the biblical narrative. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 40 times across 37 verses, with many occurrences in Genesis and Judges. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding account and the people or events connected with that location.

This noun refers to a talent, a large unit of value represented as “10,000 dollars.” In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it is used for amounts of wealth or payment, helping express the size of a financial sum. The word occurs 61 times in the LXX corpus, across 48 verses, and is rendered “talent” where translation evidence is available. Its exact amount in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

e.h: A Greek LXX Word for Grave
e.t: This noun means “grave,” referring to the place where a dead person is buried. It names a physical burial place rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 47 times, showing that this is a recurring word for burial locations. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and how the grave is being mentioned there.

This adjective describes someone as “thrice-unhappy,” expressing an intensified condition of deep misery or distress. The word applies a strong negative description to a person or subject rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 16:6. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a heightened expression of unhappiness.

This Greek LXX preposition means “under” or “by,” expressing position beneath something or association with a person or agent. It commonly connects one thing with what is below it, or indicates that something happens by someone’s agency. The word occurs 441 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its precise force depends on the phrase and surrounding context. Its central idea remains a relationship of subordination, location, or agency.

This verb means to “play-act”: to behave as though one is taking on a role instead of simply showing what is genuine. It describes performed or assumed behavior, with the exact force determined by the surrounding sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages in Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Because the individual verse texts are not included here, this entry explains the word’s ordinary meaning rather than its particular force in any one passage.

This noun describes “deliberation after the facts; remorse”—regretful thinking that comes only after an action or decision, when someone looks back and wishes better judgment had come earlier. It names the painful realization that careful thought arrived too late, rather than beforehand. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Proverbs 31:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on belated reflection and remorse.

This LXX noun refers to a low, petty quality described as “meanness” or “paltriness.” It points to something contemptibly small, base, or lacking dignity rather than something noble or substantial. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 4:12. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is a condition of low character or worth.

This adjective describes someone who is “fond of women.” It characterizes a person by an inclination or affection directed toward women, rather than naming an action or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at 1 Kings 11:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a personal disposition of fondness toward women.

This noun means “tender love” or “affectionateness”—warm, caring devotion toward another person. It describes love marked by genuine fondness and heartfelt concern, rather than merely stating that someone loves. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains consistent across these uses: a deeply affectionate bond expressed from the heart.

This adjective means “blazing,” describing something burning brightly or intensely. It adds the quality of strong, vivid fire to the person or thing being described. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 3:24. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is something marked by intense flame or brilliant burning.

This Greek LXX adjective describes someone or something that is “tributary to” another or “paying tribute to” another. It identifies a subject connected with tribute—an imposed payment or obligation owed to a superior authority. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, at Deuteronomy 20:11, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “handcuff,” referring to a restraint placed around the hands. It describes a physical means of limiting someone’s freedom or movement, and it can be used in passages about people being restrained, subdued, or held under authority. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, including Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“Gold” names the metal itself and can also describe something made of or associated with gold. In the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical writings, it functions as both a noun and an adjective. This word appears 19 times in the LXX corpus, including passages from Kings, Ezra, Job, Proverbs, Sirach, and Wisdom. Its central meaning remains straightforward: gold as a material or a description of something golden. Context determines what object or feature is being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “lie”: to speak falsely or present something untrue. It describes the act of lying rather than a person or object. The word appears 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including passages from Deuteronomy, Samuel, Job, Psalms, and Susanna. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding statement, but its basic sense remains the deliberate expression of what is false.
